fixes.explanation: That's it. After Rehoboam had established his sovereignty and royal power, he and all Israel with him forsook the Law of the LORD (2 Chronicles 12:1). The power was in place, and the Law still got left behind. I think that's the sneaky part, friend: it happened after his rule was established.

No treaty in this passage, baker. Egypt does show up, but with an army, and we'll get to that. What verse 1 says is that Rehoboam and all Israel with him forsook the Law of the LORD (2 Chronicles 12:1). A treaty isn't what that verse mentions.

Babylon doesn't show up here, baker. Shishak is king of Egypt, and his army comes out of Egypt (2 Chronicles 12:2-3). Libyans, Sukkites and Cushites come with him. Those big empires are easy to mix up, friend.

The text says the opposite. Shishak captured the fortified cities of Judah and came as far as Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 12:4). Rehoboam had built up cities like those earlier (2 Chronicles 11:5). So those cities were captured, friend.

You got it, baker. Shemaiah the prophet tells them, “This is what the LORD says: ‘You have forsaken Me; therefore, I have forsaken you into the hand of Shishak.’…” (2 Chronicles 12:5) It's a hard word to hear. But the LORD tells them plainly what's going on.

No gold deal in the LORD's word. What Shemaiah the prophet says is “You have forsaken Me; therefore, I have forsaken you into the hand of Shishak.” (2 Chronicles 12:5) Nothing there about paying anybody off. The word names the reason, baker: they had forsaken Him.
Humble is right. The leaders of Israel and the king humbled themselves and said, “The LORD is righteous.” (2 Chronicles 12:6) I tell you, friend, I think saying that out loud takes some guts.

Defend isn't the word, baker. The text says the leaders of Israel and the king humbled themselves and said, “The LORD is righteous.” (2 Chronicles 12:6) That's what the verse gives us: they humbled themselves, and those words.
Hide isn't the word, friend. The leaders of Israel and the king humbled themselves and said, “The LORD is righteous.” (2 Chronicles 12:6) Humbled is what the verse says, so that's the one that fits.

False is right. The king and the leaders humbled themselves and said, “The LORD is righteous.” (2 Chronicles 12:6) Saying He is righteous is the opposite of calling Him unfair. I think that's a good sign they heard Him.

Yes, baker. When the LORD saw that they had humbled themselves, He told Shemaiah, “They have humbled themselves; I will not destroy them, but will soon grant them deliverance.” (2 Chronicles 12:7) The word from the LORD came after they humbled themselves. Humbling themselves matters.

That's not what the LORD says, friend. He tells Shemaiah, “My wrath will not be poured out on Jerusalem through Shishak.” (2 Chronicles 12:7) He also says, “I will not destroy them…” Those are the words He gave, and letting Jerusalem burn isn't one of them.

Nothing about scattering in this word, baker. The LORD told Shemaiah, “They have humbled themselves; I will not destroy them, but will soon grant them deliverance.” (2 Chronicles 12:7) Scattering isn't in it. The word is about sparing them.
Not silver, baker. Rehoboam made bronze shields to replace the gold ones Shishak took (2 Chronicles 12:9-10). Silver isn't mentioned in this passage at all. Gold out, bronze in.

True. Whenever the king entered the house of the LORD, the guards would go with him, bearing the shields, and later they would return them to the guardroom (2 Chronicles 12:11). Those bronze shields had a whole routine. Out with the king, then back to the guardroom.

The text says it's true, baker. Whenever the king entered the house of the LORD, the guards would go with him, bearing the shields, and later they would return them to the guardroom (2 Chronicles 12:11). The guards carry them out whenever the king goes in, and back they go. That's the pattern the verse gives, friend.

Nope, friend. The text says that because Rehoboam humbled himself, the anger of the LORD turned away from him, and He did not destroy him completely (2 Chronicles 12:12). Nothing about the anger being moved onto Shishak. Not in this verse, baker.

You'd think so after an attack, baker. But the text says, “Indeed, conditions were good in Judah.” (2 Chronicles 12:12) The LORD's anger turned away from Rehoboam. Hopeless doesn't fit that picture at all.

That's the reason the writer gives: “And Rehoboam did evil because he did not set his heart to seek the LORD.” (2 Chronicles 12:14) The reason is about the heart, not about armies or allies. I think that's worth sitting with, friend.

The text doesn't say that, baker. The writer gives the reason plainly: “And Rehoboam did evil because he did not set his heart to seek the LORD.” (2 Chronicles 12:14) Egypt's gods aren't mentioned in this passage at all. The reason given is that he did not set his heart to seek the LORD.

No priests of Jeroboam in this verse, friend. The writer says, “And Rehoboam did evil because he did not set his heart to seek the LORD.” (2 Chronicles 12:14) That's a short sentence carrying a lot, baker. The writer points straight at the heart.

The text says the opposite, baker. There was war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam throughout their days (2 Chronicles 12:15). Jeroboam was the king of Israel (1 Kings 12:20). So peace isn't what the verse gives us.

False is right. “There was war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam throughout their days.” (2 Chronicles 12:15) Jeroboam was the king of Israel (1 Kings 12:20). So even with conditions good in Judah (2 Chronicles 12:12), the writer still records war between them.

Abijah is right. When Rehoboam rested with his fathers and was buried in the City of David, his son Abijah reigned in his place (2 Chronicles 12:16). Rehoboam had other sons too (2 Chronicles 11:18-20). This one took the throne.
